issues.subcategory: Construct definition contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript defines moral incongruence in the introduction and literature review as 'the interaction of moral disapproval and use frequency,' but in the Present Study section it redefines the key predictor as 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' These are fundamentally different operationalizations. Severity of consequences is an outcome-adjacent variable, not a frequency measure, and conflating the two undermines the entire conceptual framework being tested.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent effect size conversions
issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d values that are inconsistent with the reported f2 and ΔR2 values. For the smallest effect, it reports ΔR2=.012, f2=.016, Cohen's d=.22 in one place, then ΔR2=.012, f2=.016, Cohen's d=.25 in another place for what appears to be the same study. Additionally, Cohen's d is not a standard metric for regression interactions; the conversion formula used is unclear and likely incorrect. For the moderate effect, ΔR2=.072 and f2=.12 are reported with Cohen's d=.69, but f2=ΔR2/(1-R2) requires knowing total R2, and the d conversion from f2 does not straightforwardly yield .69.
issues.quote: Prior studies of moral incongruence have found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen's d = .97, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020) effects... Given this variability, we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: SESOI derivation inconsistency
issues.description: The SESOI is set at δ=|.11| based on a β=.11 from a study using religiousness (not moral disapproval) as the moderator and a different outcome measure (CPUI-4, not BPS). The authors themselves acknowledge this is a different operationalization. They then note that when the BPS was used in that same study, β=.145, and in a more parallel study β=.270. Using the least parallel, most conservative estimate as the SESOI for equivalence testing creates an asymmetric test that strongly favors finding equivalence for non-pornography behaviors, biasing results toward confirming the authors' preferred hypothesis.
issues.quote: Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency in predicting self-reported addiction. Additionally, this past work used a different and less rigorously validated outcome measure than those proposed for the current study (Cyber Pornography Use Inventory-4; Grubbs & Gola, 2019). Within the same study, when the BPS (as proposed above) was used as an outcome, the standardized estimate (β value) obtained for the interaction of religiousness and use was higher (β = .145). Similarly, in a past U.S. national sample... the observed standardized estimate was substantially larger (β = .270). Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: Oversampling confound in gambling analyses
issues.description: The gambling sample combines a nationally representative sample (n=2,500) with a sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500) recruited specifically because of their gambling behavior. This creates a severely biased gambling subsample that is not representative of the general population. Moral disapproval of gambling will be systematically lower in the sports-wagering oversample (since they actively gamble), and problem gambling severity will be higher. Combining these samples without appropriate weighting or stratified analysis will distort the moral incongruence interaction for gambling, making it impossible to compare gambling results to pornography results on equal footing.
issues.quote: Due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Non-equivalent outcome measures across behaviors
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are assessed using validated, behavior-specific scales (BPS and PGSI respectively) in addition to modified NIDA-ASSIST items, while all substance use outcomes rely solely on modified NIDA-ASSIST items that have not been validated for those substances in this modified form. This creates a fundamental asymmetry: the primary outcomes for the two behaviors the authors most want to compare (pornography vs. gambling/substances) are measured with different instruments of different psychometric quality. Comparing interaction effect sizes across behaviors measured with non-equivalent instruments is methodologically inappropriate.
issues.quote: In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen (Kraus et al., 2020)... In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001).

issues.subcategory: Contradictory scale anchors for NIDA-ASSIST items
issues.description: The methods text states that problematic use questions will be answered 'on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day),' but the supplemental materials show the Friend/Family Concern and Failure to Control items use a 3-point scale (0=No Never; 3=Yes, but not in past 3 months; 6=Yes, in past 3 months). Averaging items with a 0-5 scale together with items scored 0, 3, or 6 is psychometrically inappropriate and will produce a composite with distorted weighting. The text describes this as taking 'the average of responses' without acknowledging the scale incompatibility.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions 'Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?' and 'Have you ever tried and failed to control, cut down or stop using or engaging in the following?' for each substance on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest.

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency scale anchor inconsistency
issues.description: The methods text states pornography viewing frequency will be assessed 'on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day),' but the supplemental materials show the actual scale anchors as Never (0) through More than Once Per Day (5), a 0-5 scale. This is inconsistent with the described 1-6 scale. The same inconsistency appears for gambling frequency. This matters for centering and interaction term computation described in the analytic plan.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods text states PGSI responses will be 'averaged,' but the PGSI is a validated instrument with a standard summed scoring protocol (total scores 0-27) with established clinical cutoffs (0=non-problem, 1-2=low risk, 3-7=moderate risk, 8+=problem gambling). Averaging rather than summing changes the metric and makes results incomparable to the established literature. Furthermore, the supplemental materials show the PGSI response options as Never(0), Sometimes(2), Most of the time(4), Almost Always(5), which is non-standard—the validated PGSI uses Never(0), Sometimes(1), Most of the time(2), Almost Always(3).
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions (e.g., 'Have you felt that you might have a problem with gambling?' and 'Has gambling caused you any health problems, including stress or anxiety?') on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods text states BPS responses are on 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' and that 'responses are summed,' but the supplemental materials show the actual response options as Never(0), Occasionally(2), Very Often(4)—a non-standard scoring where the middle option is scored 2 and the highest is scored 4, yielding a possible range of 0-20, not 0-10 as would be expected from a 0-2 scale summed across 5 items. This discrepancy between the described and actual scoring is a significant internal inconsistency.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?' by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors (e.g., 'You have attempted to "cut back" or stop using pornography, but were unsuccessful.') on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: Moral incongruence operationalization mismatch
issues.description: The theoretical definition of moral incongruence requires that a person both engages in a behavior AND morally disapproves of it—the interaction captures the amplification of use-addiction links by disapproval. However, the study administers moral disapproval measures to ALL participants regardless of whether they engage in the behavior. Non-users who morally disapprove of a behavior are included in the interaction term computation, which is conceptually incoherent: a non-user cannot experience moral incongruence about a behavior they do not engage in. This inflates the sample for interaction analyses with participants for whom the construct is theoretically inapplicable.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency aggregation problem
issues.description: The methods state that 'to form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken,' but the supplemental materials show only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). There are no multiple gambling behavior items to average across. This is either an error in the methods description or a missing set of items in the supplemental materials. If only one item is used, the averaging description is misleading; if multiple items were intended, they are absent from the protocol.
issues.quote: Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale described above, ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day). To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: Causal language from cross-sectional design
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, the authors use causal language ('moral incongruence predicts,' 'moral disapproval amplifies,' 'moral incongruence is driving feelings of addiction') while acknowledging in the limitations that the design is cross-sectional. The hypotheses are framed as causal tests, and the implications section discusses what findings would 'demonstrate' about causal mechanisms. Cross-sectional moderation analyses cannot establish temporal precedence or rule out reverse causation (e.g., feeling addicted may cause people to morally disapprove of their behavior).
issues.quote: Ultimately, the PPMI model implies two strong claims regarding the role of moral incongruence in predicting self-perceived feelings of addiction... moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use.

issues.subcategory: Unaddressed confounding in moral disapproval-addiction link
issues.description: The manuscript does not adequately address the possibility that moral disapproval and self-reported addiction symptoms share common causes (e.g., general negative affect, neuroticism, shame proneness, or religious identity) that would produce spurious correlations between them. The covariates included (age, gender, religiousness) are insufficient to rule out these confounds. Religiousness is included as a covariate but is also theorized as the primary driver of moral disapproval, creating a potential suppression or multicollinearity issue that is not discussed.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates, as prior work has demonstrated clear links between such variables and self-reported problematic pornography use.

issues.subcategory: Inadequate power for key subgroup analyses
issues.description: The power analysis reveals that for prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140) and illicit drug use (estimated n=240-480), the study is severely underpowered to detect the SESOI (f2=.015), with achieved power of .301 and .472-.764 respectively. The authors acknowledge this but propose an ad hoc solution of changing the equivalence region for these substances. This means the study cannot test its primary hypothesis (equivalence with null) for two of the five substance categories, fundamentally limiting the scope of the conclusions that can be drawn.
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc equivalence region redefinition
issues.description: The analytic plan specifies that if results for gambling and substances exceed the primary equivalence region, the authors will redefine the equivalence region using the lower bound of the 95% CI from the pornography interaction. This is a pre-specified but highly flexible analytic decision that essentially guarantees some form of 'support' for the hypothesis regardless of outcome. The choice of which CI bound to use (lower vs. upper) and which reference study to use for this secondary equivalence region is not fully justified and introduces researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Unspecified handling of OLS assumption violations
issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate,' but does not specify what 'substantially violated' means, what alternative analyses will be used, or what criteria will determine whether to present OLS or alternative results. This leaves substantial researcher discretion in the analysis pipeline that could influence results, particularly given that ordinal outcome measures (averaged Likert items) are likely to violate normality assumptions.
issues.quote: Although Ordinary Least Squares techniques (such as the moderation analyses conducted by the Interactive application) in large sample sizes are often robust against some violations (Schmidt & Finan, 2018), in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: Missing multiple comparison correction plan
issues.description: The study conducts 8 moderation analyses (plus additional direct effect tests) across multiple behaviors and substances. No correction for multiple comparisons is mentioned or planned. With 8 interaction tests at α=.05, the familywise error rate is approximately 34%. The authors mention Holm-adjusted statistics only for bivariate correlations, not for the primary moderation analyses. This is particularly problematic given that the study's conclusions depend on finding a significant interaction for pornography but null interactions for other behaviors.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: Missing plan for handling the sports-wagering oversample in non-gambling analyses
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify how the sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500) will be handled in analyses for non-gambling behaviors (pornography, substance use). If included, this non-representative subsample will distort the nationally representative analyses. If excluded, the effective sample sizes for non-gambling analyses differ from those reported in the power analysis. No weighting scheme or exclusion criteria for the oversample in non-gambling analyses is described.
issues.quote: Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Unspecified centering procedure for interaction terms
issues.description: The analytic plan states that 'focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated' in SPSS, but then states 'For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.' These two statements are contradictory—it is unclear whether centered or raw variables will be used to compute the interaction term, which affects interpretation of main effects in the moderation model.
issues.quote: Additionally, focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated... For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: Absence of pre-registration link or OSF identifier
issues.description: Despite being described as a Registered Report, the manuscript does not provide a pre-registration link, OSF project identifier, or any verifiable record of where the registration is housed. For a Registered Report, the pre-registration is the foundational document establishing the confirmatory nature of the analyses. Without this, readers cannot verify that the analytic plan was indeed pre-specified or assess any deviations from it.
issues.quote: The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence (the interaction of behavioral frequency and moral disapproval of a behavior) is uniquely related to sexual behavior, or if it generalizes to other addictions as well.

issues.subcategory: Missing psychometric validation plan for modified ASSIST
issues.description: The authors substantially modify the NIDA-ASSIST by adding new behaviors (pornography, gambling), changing response scales, and creating composite scores by averaging items with incompatible scales. No plan is provided to evaluate the psychometric properties of these modifications before using them as primary outcome measures. While the authors mention calculating Cronbach's alpha and omega, they do not plan confirmatory factor analyses or other validation steps to ensure the modified instrument measures what it purports to measure.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim of U.S. representativeness given oversample inclusion
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the sample as 'nationally representative' but the total sample of 4,000 includes 1,500 sports-wagering individuals who are explicitly not representative of the general population. The nationally representative component is only n=2,500. Describing the combined sample as representative is misleading, and the power analyses use the combined N=4,000 for gambling analyses, inflating apparent power for a non-representative gambling subsample.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms... This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate extrapolation to clinical populations
issues.description: The discussion and implications sections draw conclusions about CSBD diagnosis and clinical practice from a community/population sample. The authors acknowledge this limitation briefly but then proceed to make strong claims about diagnostic validity and the ICD-11 criteria. Community samples systematically underrepresent clinical severity, and moral incongruence effects may operate differently in treatment-seeking populations where true dysregulation is more prevalent.
issues.quote: Should results confirm the above hypotheses, this work would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD. Chiefly, should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model.

issues.subcategory: Confirmation bias in hypothesis framing
issues.description: The study is explicitly framed as aiming to 'demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors' and to provide 'strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI.' This is not a neutral test of competing hypotheses but a confirmatory study designed to support a specific theoretical position. The equivalence testing approach is asymmetric: a significant interaction for pornography confirms the theory, while null interactions for other behaviors also confirm the theory. There is no pre-specified outcome that would clearly falsify the PPMI model.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of moral incongruence to non-sexual behaviors
issues.description: The theoretical basis for why moral incongruence should be unique to sexual behavior is not adequately developed. The authors assert uniqueness based on the ICD-11 caveat and religious conservatism literature, but do not provide a theoretical mechanism explaining why the interaction of moral disapproval and frequency would specifically amplify addiction feelings for sexual behaviors but not for substances or gambling. The hypothesis of uniqueness is empirical but lacks theoretical grounding beyond circular reasoning (it's unique because the ICD-11 says so).
issues.quote: The claim is that the relationship between moral incongruence and self-reported feelings of addiction, compulsivity, or dysregulation is unique to sexual behaviors, particularly pornography use. This general observation is based on past literature that has consistently noted that religiously conservative individuals are especially likely to report experiencing problems with compulsive or addictive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of moral disapproval direct effect with moral incongruence interaction
issues.description: The hypotheses include both direct effect predictions (moral disapproval predicts addiction symptoms) and interaction predictions (moral disapproval × frequency predicts addiction symptoms) for all behaviors. The authors predict that direct effects will be significant for gambling and substances but interactions will not. This creates a theoretical inconsistency: if moral disapproval directly predicts addiction feelings for gambling and substances, this itself constitutes a form of moral incongruence (disapproval-driven distress), undermining the claim that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems, even when including gambling frequency, religiousness, gender, and age as covariates in a regression model. However, we do not expect to find that the interaction of moral disapproval of gambling and gambling frequency will significantly predict self-reported gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Unjustified assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The manuscript states 'we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data' based solely on YouGov's proprietary quality control processes. This is an unrealistic assumption for a survey covering sensitive topics (substance use, pornography, gambling). No plan is provided for handling missing data should it occur, including no specification of whether listwise deletion, multiple imputation, or other methods would be used. This is particularly concerning given that sensitive items (e.g., illicit drug use, pornography) are likely to have higher non-response rates.
issues.quote: As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling skip-logic non-response
issues.description: The study uses skip logic where only past-year users complete problematic use measures. However, the manuscript states measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This creates an internal contradiction: if non-users complete problematic use measures, their responses (presumably all zeros) will be included in analyses, artificially inflating the sample size and distorting distributions. If non-users are excluded, this constitutes planned missingness that requires explicit handling in the analytic plan.
issues.quote: Like the above-described process for the ASSIST, only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months (i.e., scores > 1 on the frequency measure) will complete the remaining items described below... For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.

issues.subcategory: Alcohol frequency measure inconsistency
issues.description: The methods describe two different alcohol frequency measures: a general frequency question ('how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed') and gender-specific heavy drinking questions (4+ drinks for women, 5+ drinks for men). It is not specified which measure will be used as the 'frequency' variable in the moral incongruence interaction for alcohol. Using general frequency versus heavy drinking frequency would yield substantially different results and represents an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen asks men to report alcohol frequency in terms of how many days they have consumed five or more drinks in a day and women to report alcohol frequency in terms of days they have consumed four or more drinks per day. Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: Absence of manipulation or attention checks
issues.description: For a study relying entirely on self-report measures of sensitive behaviors (pornography use, substance use, gambling) and moral attitudes, no attention checks or validity indicators beyond YouGov's proprietary standards are planned. The authors explicitly state they do not anticipate needing to remove inattentive responses, but provide no criteria for identifying or handling such responses if they occur. This is particularly important for sensitive topics where social desirability responding is a known concern.
issues.quote: Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measure limitations
issues.description: Moral disapproval for all behaviors is assessed with a single item ('I believe that [behavior] is morally wrong'). Single-item measures have well-documented reliability limitations and cannot capture the multidimensional nature of moral attitudes (e.g., disgust-based vs. harm-based moral disapproval, personal vs. social moral norms). The manuscript does not acknowledge this limitation or justify the use of single items despite the centrality of moral disapproval to the entire theoretical framework being tested.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy in number of moderation analyses
issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest,' but Table 1 lists 7 target substances/behaviors (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, pornography, gambling). The text elsewhere mentions 7 behaviors. The discrepancy between 7 and 8 is unexplained and may reflect an uncounted behavior or a counting error.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

issues.subcategory: Covariates obtained from panel data without measurement details
issues.description: Age and gender are described as obtained from YouGov panel data rather than assessed in the survey, but no information is provided about how these variables are operationalized in the panel (e.g., whether gender is binary or includes non-binary options, whether age is continuous or categorical). The analytic plan specifies 'gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male)' which collapses all non-male genders into a single category, but this decision is not justified or discussed in terms of its implications for the analyses.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey)... Interactions will be tested using this program with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.subcategory: Religiousness measure direction transformation not pre-validated
issues.description: The religiousness composite is constructed by averaging three standardized items and then multiplying by -1 to reverse the direction. This transformation is described but the psychometric properties of this composite (reliability, factor structure) are not reported or planned to be evaluated. Additionally, the three items include different response scales (4-point importance scale, 7-point prayer frequency scale, 6-point attendance scale) that are standardized before averaging, but the justification for treating these as indicators of a single latent construct is not provided.
issues.quote: Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center (Pew Research Center, 2015)... In their raw form, lower response values correspond to greater religiousness. Accordingly, upon taking the average of standardized responses to the above three questions, the average will be transformed by multiplying by -1 so that higher scores correspond to higher religiousness.
